title: Gaza ceasefire could collapse without urgent action, Board of Peace tells UN Security Council
dek: In its latest report to the Council, the US-backed board says Israel is blocking Gaza's interim administration, police and winter aid, and that Israeli strikes and Hamas military activity have stalled the plan.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
The US-backed Board of Peace, set up to oversee the Gaza ceasefire and the territory's reconstruction, has warned the UN Security Council that the year-old truce between Israel and Hamas may not survive unless both sides carry out what they agreed. "A ceasefire that delivers nothing visible cannot be sustained indefinitely," the board said in a report submitted to the Council on Tuesday, 17 November, according to reports from a copy of the document.

The report puts much of the blame for the stalled plan on the Israeli government. It says Israel has not allowed the Palestinian technocratic administration created to run Gaza on an interim basis to begin work, has not taken the decisions needed to train and deploy a civilian police force, and is restricting the supplies Gazans need to get through the winter. It also says continued Israeli strikes and Hamas military activity have together stopped progress on the road map. The board asked the Council to press both sides to meet their commitments.

## What the report says

The board describes "the distance between what has been agreed and what is happening on the ground" as "the principal risk to the process", according to reports.

On governance, it says the interim technocratic administration has still not been allowed into the territory. The board argues that Israel's slowness in granting approvals is, in effect, leaving Hamas in charge of Gaza, one report said.

On security, it says Israel has not decided how civilian police are to be trained, deployed and returned to Gaza, and calls on the Israeli government to decide "without delay". That gap has in turn held up the International Stabilization Force, which the plan relies on to allow an Israeli withdrawal, the disarmament of Hamas and large-scale reconstruction.

On aid, the report says "restrictions imposed by Israel on the entry of supplies and equipment", together with funding shortfalls, have hampered preparations for winter. It asks for "scaled-up entry of shelter and winterization materials" and for approval of pumps, generators and heavy machinery, and warns that Palestinians face "another winter in tents and rubble". About 70,000 tents were flooded by heavy rain earlier this month, according to reports.

The board's message to both parties was the same: "Neither party may treat the other's delay as license for its own inaction." It also said that the end result "must lead to the credible pathway to Palestinian self-determination and statehood", and that no unilateral step should be allowed to close it off. If the ceasefire collapses, it warned, there would be no road map, no administration and no conditions for rebuilding.

## What each side says

There was no immediate public response to the report from Israel's government or from Hamas. Israel has said it has taken steps to address the winter crisis in Gaza, according to reports. Ron Dermer, a former close aide to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and a former strategic affairs minister, has urged Israel to "give a shot" to the board, pointing out that the ceasefire already requires Hamas to disarm and Gaza to be demilitarised; the board shared his remarks approvingly, one report said.

Hamas accepted the board's plan for disarming its fighters on 30 July. Progress has since stalled; Israel argues the plan would not make Hamas give up all its weapons, according to reports.

Israeli strikes have continued throughout the truce. More than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza since October 2023, according to figures from Gaza's health ministry cited in reports; the figures cannot be independently verified and do not distinguish between civilians and fighters.

## Background

The ceasefire took effect on 10 October 2025 under a 20-point plan put forward by US President Donald Trump. On 17 November 2025, a year to the day before this report, the Security Council adopted Resolution 2803 by 13 votes to none, with China and Russia abstaining. The resolution endorsed the plan, welcomed the Board of Peace as a transitional administration for Gaza, authorised a temporary International Stabilization Force, and asked the board to report to the Council every six months. The authorisation runs until 31 December 2027 unless the Council decides otherwise.

The board's first report, delivered in May by its senior envoy Nickolay Mladenov, already said the process was stuck over the question of disarming Hamas.

Israel's own politics are now in flux. The 27 October election left neither Mr Netanyahu's bloc nor the opposition led by former army chief Gadi Eisenkot with a majority in the 120-seat Knesset. On Tuesday, the same day the report reached the Council, the Knesset elected Matan Kahana, an ally of Mr Eisenkot, as Speaker by 66 votes to 52, according to reports. Mr Eisenkot is trying to form a government, and Mr Netanyahu leads the outgoing one.

## Why it matters for India

India has backed the plan but has not joined the board. It attended the board's first meeting in Washington in February as an observer, and the Ministry of External Affairs said then that India supported Mr Trump's Gaza peace initiative and all efforts under Resolution 2803. India's stated position remains support for a sovereign, independent and viable Palestinian state based on the 1967 borders, living side by side with Israel.

A breakdown in Gaza would add to the strain on a region already at war around the Strait of Hormuz, where Iranian and US forces have traded strikes this week and an Indian sailor is missing after an attack on a tanker. The Gulf is home to millions of Indian workers and supplies much of India's oil and gas, and New Delhi's plans for the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor depend on a stable Israel and Arab world.

## What happens next

The Security Council has not yet announced a date to discuss the report. The board's next six-monthly report is due in May 2027. In Israel, the shape of the next government, and its willingness to approve the interim administration, police deployment and stabilisation force, is likely to decide whether the plan moves forward.

## Timeline

- 10 October 2025: Gaza ceasefire takes effect under the US 20-point plan.
- 17 November 2025: Security Council adopts Resolution 2803, endorsing the plan and the Board of Peace.
- February 2026: India attends the board's first meeting in Washington as an observer.
- May 2026: First board report says the process is deadlocked over Hamas disarmament.
- 30 July 2026: Hamas accepts the board's disarmament plan.
- 27 October 2026: Israel's election produces no majority.
- 17 November 2026: Latest board report warns the ceasefire could collapse.
